screens.title: Contract Verification & Etherscan
screens.narratorSegment: When you deploy a smart contract, the blockchain stores bytecode that humans cannot read. Verification is the process of publishing your original Solidity source, compiler options, and constructor inputs to a block explorer so it can recompile and prove the on-chain bytecode matches your source. This matters because verified contracts let users, integrators, and auditors inspect the exact logic behind transactions, improving trust and simplifying debugging. In this lesson you will learn both the why and the how: first, the transparency and security benefits verification provides; then concrete steps using Hardhat's Etherscan plugin and Foundry's verification commands. We'll also explore the common stumbling blocks—mismatched compiler settings, missing constructor arguments, and network mismatches—and how to resolve them. By the end, you'll be able to verify a simple Greeter or token contract on Sepolia and understand how verification supports safe interactions and third-party integrations. Think of verification as publishing a readable blueprint that proves your deployed object is what you claim. That blueprint is what others will rely on when they build, audit, or interact with your contract.

screens.title: What is contract verification?
screens.narratorSegment: Contract verification is the act of publishing your contract's original source code, compiler configuration, and constructor arguments to a block explorer so it can recompile and compare the generated bytecode to what is deployed on-chain. Mechanically, the explorer compiles using the supplied settings and then performs a precise equality check. If the recompiled bytecode and the on-chain bytecode are identical, the explorer marks the contract as verified and displays the source code. This is not a superficial check. It confirms that the human-readable source you provide is the exact code that produced the machine-level bytes on the blockchain. A concrete example: you deployed a simple Greeter contract that stores a string provided to the constructor. By uploading the Greeter. sol source, the exact compiler version, optimizer runs, and the constructor argument string, the explorer reproduces the same bytecode and confirms verification. A common misconception is that verification is optional decoration; in practice, verification unlocks explorer features like the transaction debugger and a direct read/write interface. Key caveats: the constructor arguments are part of the bytecode payload, optimizer settings change code generation, and linked libraries alter binary output. Your takeaway: verification is a reproducible proof that your source equals the deployed artifact.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › What is verification?
Definition & mechanics

Verification uploads source, compiler options, and constructor args so the explorer can recompile and compare bytecode.

Key bullets
  • Explorer recompiles your source with provided settings and compares output to on-chain bytes.
  • Constructor arguments and optimizer settings directly influence the generated bytecode.
  • Successful match marks the contract as verified and shows readable source to the public.
Key Takeaway

Verification is a reproducible check: identical compiler settings and constructor inputs produce identical bytecode.

Concrete example: Greeter
// Greeter.sol
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract Greeter {
  string public greeting;
  constructor(string memory _greeting) { greeting = _greeting; }
  function greet() public view returns (string memory) { return greeting; }
}
Provide the exact constructor string, the compiler version used, and optimizer runs. When the explorer recompiles the source with those settings, it must produce the same bytes stored during deployment.
Common misconception
Verification is not cosmetic; it unlocks explorer tools and proves provenance. Failing to verify hides the logic and reduces trust.

screens.title: Verification workflow steps
screens.narratorSegment: Verification follows a predictable sequence of steps that you can treat as a checklist. First, you deploy the contract to a public network; this writes bytecode to the blockchain. Second, collect the exact compiler version, optimizer settings, and EVM version used during compilation. Third, gather constructor arguments exactly as supplied during deployment—strings as strings, integers as strings, and addresses as checksummed strings. Fourth, choose your tool: Hardhat or Foundry, and configure the block explorer A P I key. Fifth, run the verification command for your tool and supply the chain and arguments. Finally, inspect the explorer response and the contract page; a match will display a green verified badge and the readable source. A concrete example: deploy Greeter to Sepolia with "Hello, Cohortia!" then run the Hardhat verify command with that exact string. A common pitfall is assuming defaults; if your local config differs from the deployment compilation settings, verification will fail. Treat the workflow as a strict recipe where each ingredient must match. This process mindset makes troubleshooting systematic and efficient. Verification workflow steps means treat verification as a strict recipe: deploy, collect exact settings and args, run the verifier, and confirm the explorer match.. In practical terms, step-by-step flow from deployment to verified source on etherscan.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Verification workflow
1. Deploy
Contract bytecode is written to the chain when you deploy from your tool.
2. Collect compilation details
Record solidity version, optimizer enabled and runs, and EVM version used for the build.
3. Gather constructor args
Provide strings, addresses, and uints in the exact order and format used at deploy time.
4. Run verifier
Use Hardhat or Foundry verification commands with your API key and chain target.
Concrete example (Hardhat)
npx hardhat verify --network sepolia 0x123...abc "Hello, Cohortia!"
If this command fails, revisit the checklist: did you use the same compiler version and optimizer runs? Did you supply the constructor string exactly as deployed?
Common mistake
Passing a non-checksummed address or an unencoded uint can cause verification to fail. Always format values as the tool expects.

screens.title: Verifying with Hardhat
screens.narratorSegment: Hardhat simplifies verification with a dedicated plugin that connects to Etherscan's A P I. Start by installing the @nomicfoundation/hardhat-etherscan package as a dev dependency, then configure the etherscan. apiKey field in your hardhat. config. js or hardhat. config. ts, usually sourcing the key from an environment variable. After deployment, run the verify task with the network flag and the deployed address followed by constructor arguments in the same order and format used at deployment. For example, verifying a Greeter deployed to Sepolia would look like: npx hardhat verify --network sepolia 0x123... abc "Hello, Cohortia!". Important details: Hardhat will normally use the compiler settings defined in its config, so ensure those entries match the build that produced the deployed bytecode. For complex projects, Hardhat's plugin often handles source flattening. If it does not, make sure imports are resolvable and no post-deploy source edits occurred. A common trap is forgetting to set the ETHERSCAN_API_KEY in your environment; that causes the A P I request to fail. The practical habit is to copy exact constructor literals from your deployment artifact and confirm your hardhat config mirrors the compiler and optimizer settings used earlier.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Verifying with Hardhat
Setup & config
Install the plugin and set ETHERSCAN_API_KEY.
// Install
npm install --save-dev @nomicfoundation/hardhat-etherscan

// hardhat.config.js
require('@nomicfoundation/hardhat-toolbox');
require('dotenv').config();
module.exports = {
  solidity: '0.8.17',
  etherscan: { apiKey: process.env.ETHERSCAN_API_KEY },
};
Ensure the solidity version and optimizer settings in hardhat.config.js are identical to those used for compiling and deploying.
Verify command
npx hardhat verify --network sepolia 0x123...abc "Hello, Cohortia!"
If your constructor takes multiple args, list them in order. Pass numbers as strings to avoid formatting surprises. Addresses should be checksummed strings.
Troubleshoot
Missing API key, wrong compiler settings, or incorrect constructor args are the usual causes of failure. Confirm each against your deployment record.

screens.title: Verifying with Foundry
screens.narratorSegment: Foundry gives you direct control via forge verify-contract and forge script with the --verify flag. Because Foundry exposes lower-level flags, you must ensure the chain id, optimizer runs, and constructor argument encoding match the original deployment. For automatic verification, running forge script with --verify will attempt verification during deployment if you provide the A P I key. For manual verification, forge verify-contract requires you to supply the contract address, contract name, chain id, number of optimizer runs, and constructor arguments encoded as ABI data. You can create those encoded args with cast abi encode. For example, to encode a single string constructor for Greeter, use cast abi encode "constructor(string)" "Hello, Foundry!" and pass the resulting hex into --constructor-args. A common misconception is that a human-readable constructor value suffices; with Foundry you often must pass the ABI-encoded form. Additionally, optimizer_runs must be set to the same value as foundry. toml used for compilation or verification will fail. Foundry's verbosity helps diagnose mismatches by showing the expected and actual bytes, which you can match against the chain to isolate the difference. Verifying with Foundry means use cast abi encode for constructor args and ensure --num-of-optimizations matches foundry.toml to avoid bytecode mismatch.. In practical terms, forge verify-contract, encoding args, and matching optimizer runs.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Verifying with Foundry
Foundry verification commands
Foundry requires explicit flags for chain id, optimizer runs, and encoded constructor args.
# Encode constructor args
cast abi encode "constructor(string)" "Hello, Foundry!"

# Verify manually
forge verify-contract  Greeter --chain-id 11155111 --num-of-optimizations 200 --constructor-args  --verifier etherscan --verifier-url https://api-sepolia.etherscan.io/api --etherscan-api-key $ETHERSCAN_API_KEY
Ensure your foundry.toml optimizer_runs entry equals the --num-of-optimizations flag. If they differ, bytecode will not match.
Common mistake
Passing unencoded constructor arguments when Foundry expects ABI-encoded values will produce a mismatch. Use cast to generate the correct payload.
Key Takeaway

Foundry gives control but requires exact flags and encoded inputs; treat those flags as part of the verification identity.

screens.title: Hardhat vs Foundry verification
screens.narratorSegment: Both Hardhat and Foundry can verify contracts, but they take slightly different approaches and afford different trade-offs. Hardhat's Etherscan plugin integrates with your build process and typically uses the compiler settings in hardhat. config. js, making verification straightforward: install the plugin, set an A P I key, and run the verify command with readable constructor arguments. Foundry, on the other hand, exposes more explicit flags and can require ABI-encoded constructor arguments for manual verification. Foundry's approach gives you fine-grained control and explicitness, but requires that you ensure flags like optimizer runs and chain id exactly match the deployment. A practical choice: if you already use Hardhat for deployment, its plugin is often the fastest path to verification. If you use Foundry for building and deploying, its native commands will feel more integrated and can be scripted inside forge scripts. Consider automation: Hardhat's verify task can be added to your deployment pipelines, while Foundry's forge script --verify can perform verification during scripted deployments. A frequent misconception is that either tool will magically handle mismatched compiler settings; neither will — you must explicitly match settings. Choose the tool that matches your build environment and make the verification settings part of your reproducible deployment recipe.

Plugin-based, uses config compiler settings, readable constructor args, easy pipeline integration.
Pros
  • Simple command syntax for verification.

screens.title: Bytecode mismatch deep dive
screens.narratorSegment: Bytecode mismatch is the most common verification failure. It means the explorer's recompiled bytes differ from the on-chain bytes. Typical root causes are: wrong compiler version, mismatched optimizer settings (enabled/disabled or runs), different EVM versions, missing or incorrectly linked libraries, or incorrect constructor arguments. To diagnose, follow a step-by-step checklist. First, compare the solidity version used in deployment to your current config. Second, check optimizer enabled and runs; even changing runs alters resulting bytecode. Third, confirm the EVM version if you specified one. Fourth, if your project uses libraries, ensure library addresses and linking were handled identically. Fifth, verify the constructor arguments are in exact order and format—use ABI encoding if required. As a concrete troubleshooting example: if the only difference is optimizer runs, recompile locally with the missing run count and verify again. A misconception is assuming whitespace or comments change the bytecode; they do not. The mismatch usually stems from compilation or linked artifact differences, not comments. Your practical fix is to reproduce the original build environment and treat verification as reproducing the binary exactly. Bytecode mismatch deep dive means systematically check solidity version, optimizer settings, evm version, library linking, and constructor arguments to resolve bytecode mismatches.. In practical terms, root causes, diagnostic checks, and step-by-step fixes.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Bytecode mismatch
Common causes
  • Compiler version differs from deployment build.
  • Optimizer enabled/disabled or runs differ.
  • Different EVM target or library linking issues.
  • Incorrect or unencoded constructor arguments.
Quick diagnostic steps
  1. Check solidity.version, optimizer settings, and evmVersion in your config.
  2. Confirm constructor args order and encoding.
  3. Rebuild artifact locally with those exact settings and compare byte length and hash.
Concrete fix example
If optimizer runs were 200 during deploy but your local project uses 100, set optimizer runs to 200, rebuild, and attempt verification again. This often resolves mismatches quickly.
Misconception
Comments and whitespace do not change bytecode; mismatches come from compilation inputs and linked artifacts.
Key Takeaway

screens.title: Privacy and safety considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Verification publishes the uncompiled source code to the public explorer, so treat what you upload as permanently visible. Never include secrets or private keys in your contract source; those belong in off-chain systems. Also be mindful of any admin keys or test-only mechanisms; if a contract contains privileged backdoors for testing, consider deploying a production build without those features. Verification improves transparency but does not replace audits; verified code still needs security reviews. A common pitfall is assuming verification implies security; verification only proves what code was deployed, not that it is secure. Practically, before publishing source, run static analysis and remove any accidental secret literals from source files. If your repository contains non-contract helper scripts that include secrets, ensure verifier inputs only include the contract source and not unrelated files. The safe practice is to treat verification as one step in a larger security checklist: publish readable source, but also audit, test extensively, and protect private keys and deployment credentials. fullNarratorScript:
When you deploy a smart contract, the blockchain stores bytecode that humans cannot read. Verification is the process of publishing your original Solidity source, compiler options, and constructor inputs to a block explorer so it can recompile and prove the on-chain bytecode matches your source. This matters because verified contracts let users, integrators, and auditors inspect the exact logic behind transactions, improving trust and simplifying debugging. In this lesson you will learn both the why and the how: first, the transparency and security benefits verification provides; then concrete steps using Hardhat's Etherscan plugin and Foundry's verification commands. We'll also explore the common stumbling blocks—mismatched compiler settings, missing constructor arguments, and network mismatches—and how to resolve them. By the end, you'll be able to verify a simple Greeter or token contract on Sepolia and understand how verification supports safe interactions and third-party integrations. Think of verification as publishing a readable blueprint that proves your deployed object is what you claim. That blueprint is what others will rely on when they build, audit, or interact with your contract.

In these objectives you'll see four concrete skills to master. First, you'll explain why verifying smart contracts on block explorers is essential for transparency and security, and be able to give examples of how verified code supports audits and user trust. Second, you'll perform verification using Hardhat's Etherscan plugin, including installing the plugin, setting an A P I key, and running the verify task with constructor arguments. Third, you'll perform verification using Foundry's verification commands, including encoding constructor arguments and matching optimizer and compiler settings. Fourth, you'll troubleshoot common verification failures: bytecode mismatch, wrong constructor arguments, missing A P I keys, and network mismatches. Each objective links a practical task to why it matters: auditors need readable source, users need confidence, and developers need predictable verification steps. You'll practice encoding constructor inputs and reading error messages so you can fix verification attempts efficiently. These objectives will guide the hands-on lab where you verify a previously deployed Greeter or token on Sepolia and resolve a simulated mismatch error.

Beyond knowing commands, you will be able to perform a verification end-to-end and explain why each piece matters. You will set up an A P I key, confirm your compiler and optimizer settings match deployment, format constructor arguments correctly, and run verification for both Hardhat and Foundry workflows. We'll also teach you how to interpret Etherscan's response and typical error messages, and how to recover from a bytecode mismatch by checking optimizer runs, EVM version, and any linked libraries. The practical assessment asks you to verify a deployed TokenVault or Greeter on Sepolia and, if a mismatch appears, to identify the most likely cause and fix it. This skill matters because verification is often a gate for public trust and for other developers to build on your work. By the end of the lab, you'll have verified a contract and practiced decoding a failure, demonstrating the competency milestone for this chapter.

Contract verification is the act of publishing your contract's original source code, compiler configuration, and constructor arguments to a block explorer so it can recompile and compare the generated bytecode to what is deployed on-chain. Mechanically, the explorer compiles using the supplied settings and then performs a precise equality check. If the recompiled bytecode and the on-chain bytecode are identical, the explorer marks the contract as verified and displays the source code. This is not a superficial check. It confirms that the human-readable source you provide is the exact code that produced the machine-level bytes on the blockchain. A concrete example: you deployed a simple Greeter contract that stores a string provided to the constructor. By uploading the Greeter. sol source, the exact compiler version, optimizer runs, and the constructor argument string, the explorer reproduces the same bytecode and confirms verification. A common misconception is that verification is optional decoration; in practice, verification unlocks explorer features like the transaction debugger and a direct read/write interface. Key caveats: the constructor arguments are part of the bytecode payload, optimizer settings change code generation, and linked libraries alter binary output. Your takeaway: verification is a reproducible proof that your source equals the deployed artifact.

Verification follows a predictable sequence of steps that you can treat as a checklist. First, you deploy the contract to a public network; this writes bytecode to the blockchain. Second, collect the exact compiler version, optimizer settings, and EVM version used during compilation. Third, gather constructor arguments exactly as supplied during deployment—strings as strings, integers as strings, and addresses as checksummed strings. Fourth, choose your tool: Hardhat or Foundry, and configure the block explorer A P I key. Fifth, run the verification command for your tool and supply the chain and arguments. Finally, inspect the explorer response and the contract page; a match will display a green verified badge and the readable source. A concrete example: deploy Greeter to Sepolia with "Hello, Cohortia!" then run the Hardhat verify command with that exact string. A common pitfall is assuming defaults; if your local config differs from the deployment compilation settings, verification will fail. Treat the workflow as a strict recipe where each ingredient must match. This process mindset makes troubleshooting systematic and efficient. Verification workflow steps means treat verification as a strict recipe: deploy, collect exact settings and args, run the verifier, and confirm the explorer match.. In practical terms, step-by-step flow from deployment to verified source on etherscan.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Hardhat simplifies verification with a dedicated plugin that connects to Etherscan's A P I. Start by installing the @nomicfoundation/hardhat-etherscan package as a dev dependency, then configure the etherscan. apiKey field in your hardhat. config. js or hardhat. config. ts, usually sourcing the key from an environment variable. After deployment, run the verify task with the network flag and the deployed address followed by constructor arguments in the same order and format used at deployment. For example, verifying a Greeter deployed to Sepolia would look like: npx hardhat verify --network sepolia 0x123... abc "Hello, Cohortia!". Important details: Hardhat will normally use the compiler settings defined in its config, so ensure those entries match the build that produced the deployed bytecode. For complex projects, Hardhat's plugin often handles source flattening. If it does not, make sure imports are resolvable and no post-deploy source edits occurred. A common trap is forgetting to set the ETHERSCAN_API_KEY in your environment; that causes the A P I request to fail. The practical habit is to copy exact constructor literals from your deployment artifact and confirm your hardhat config mirrors the compiler and optimizer settings used earlier.

Foundry gives you direct control via forge verify-contract and forge script with the --verify flag. Because Foundry exposes lower-level flags, you must ensure the chain id, optimizer runs, and constructor argument encoding match the original deployment. For automatic verification, running forge script with --verify will attempt verification during deployment if you provide the A P I key. For manual verification, forge verify-contract requires you to supply the contract address, contract name, chain id, number of optimizer runs, and constructor arguments encoded as ABI data. You can create those encoded args with cast abi encode. For example, to encode a single string constructor for Greeter, use cast abi encode "constructor(string)" "Hello, Foundry!" and pass the resulting hex into --constructor-args. A common misconception is that a human-readable constructor value suffices; with Foundry you often must pass the ABI-encoded form. Additionally, optimizer_runs must be set to the same value as foundry. toml used for compilation or verification will fail. Foundry's verbosity helps diagnose mismatches by showing the expected and actual bytes, which you can match against the chain to isolate the difference. Verifying with Foundry means use cast abi encode for constructor args and ensure --num-of-optimizations matches foundry.toml to avoid bytecode mismatch.. In practical terms, forge verify-contract, encoding args, and matching optimizer runs.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Both Hardhat and Foundry can verify contracts, but they take slightly different approaches and afford different trade-offs. Hardhat's Etherscan plugin integrates with your build process and typically uses the compiler settings in hardhat. config. js, making verification straightforward: install the plugin, set an A P I key, and run the verify command with readable constructor arguments. Foundry, on the other hand, exposes more explicit flags and can require ABI-encoded constructor arguments for manual verification. Foundry's approach gives you fine-grained control and explicitness, but requires that you ensure flags like optimizer runs and chain id exactly match the deployment. A practical choice: if you already use Hardhat for deployment, its plugin is often the fastest path to verification. If you use Foundry for building and deploying, its native commands will feel more integrated and can be scripted inside forge scripts. Consider automation: Hardhat's verify task can be added to your deployment pipelines, while Foundry's forge script --verify can perform verification during scripted deployments. A frequent misconception is that either tool will magically handle mismatched compiler settings; neither will — you must explicitly match settings. Choose the tool that matches your build environment and make the verification settings part of your reproducible deployment recipe.

Bytecode mismatch is the most common verification failure. It means the explorer's recompiled bytes differ from the on-chain bytes. Typical root causes are: wrong compiler version, mismatched optimizer settings (enabled/disabled or runs), different EVM versions, missing or incorrectly linked libraries, or incorrect constructor arguments. To diagnose, follow a step-by-step checklist. First, compare the solidity version used in deployment to your current config. Second, check optimizer enabled and runs; even changing runs alters resulting bytecode. Third, confirm the EVM version if you specified one. Fourth, if your project uses libraries, ensure library addresses and linking were handled identically. Fifth, verify the constructor arguments are in exact order and format—use ABI encoding if required. As a concrete troubleshooting example: if the only difference is optimizer runs, recompile locally with the missing run count and verify again. A misconception is assuming whitespace or comments change the bytecode; they do not. The mismatch usually stems from compilation or linked artifact differences, not comments. Your practical fix is to reproduce the original build environment and treat verification as reproducing the binary exactly. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Assume you deployed Greeter at address 0x123... abc with constructor string "Hello, Cohortia!" and that hardhat. config. js contains the same compiler and optimizer settings used for compilation. Verification publishes the uncompiled source code to the public explorer, so treat what you upload as permanently visible. Never include secrets or private keys in your contract source; those belong in off-chain systems. Also be mindful of any admin keys or test-only mechanisms; if a contract contains privileged backdoors for testing, consider deploying a production build without those features. Verification improves transparency but does not replace audits; verified code still needs security reviews. A common pitfall is assuming verification implies security; verification only proves what code was deployed, not that it is secure.
